summary: Rinker Point's 1935 30-foot L-4 tower served as a WWII aircraft-warning post, was destroyed in 1965, and sits on private timber land with no visible remains reported.

facts.status_note: Tower destroyed in 1965; the site is on private timber land and no source describes remains
facts.agency: U.S. Forest Service, Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest

access.note: On Sierra Pacific Land & Timber ground, reached through a gate off an unsigned dirt road. A 2019 visit saw no signs suggesting that hiking was not allowed.

visit.trail_note: Park at the gate at the end of the branch road, then walk about 1 mile and gain roughly 650 feet on the old road

events.note: 30-foot pole L-4 tower one mile southeast of the summit; WillhiteWeb says built on or before 1935
Panorama photos taken July 21, 1935 by George Clisby
Aircraft Warning Service station activated March 21, 1942 (Bellingham Filter Center)
AWS station deactivated October 16, 1943; the Forest Service kept using the site; a shed for sleeping quarters was built in 1943
Destroyed in 1965 per firelookout.com and the Darrington history; the FFLOS register says removed
Registered April 24, 2012 as FFLOS US 1258; nominated by Ray Kresek

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The FFLOS register says removed in 1965, while firelookout.com and the Darrington history say destroyed in 1965. The year agrees; only the verb differs.

Rex's page dates the Aircraft Warning Service activation to March 21, 1942 (Bellingham Filter Center). The Darrington history says Rinker began serving as an AWS station in 1943, the year its sleeping-quarters shed was built. The story attributes the 1942 date to Rex's page.

notes_for_editor: Elevation conflicts and is not explained by the sources: 3,090 ft in the FFLOS register and the Darrington history vs 2,620 ft in WillhiteWeb's site details, so the story gives no elevation. The record coordinates match the FFLOS point; WillhiteWeb places the tower about a mile southeast of Rinker Point, so a human should check whether the record point is the tower site or the summit. Exact site is uncertain (WillhiteWeb's 2018 and 2019 visits found no evidence). Removed vs destroyed wording differs; the year agrees. AWS detail comes from secondary transcriptions (Rex's page, WillhiteWeb, Darrington history). No new photos added.
